analysis.problem_summary: Remove all nodes from a singly-linked list whose values match a given integer target `val`, and return the head of the updated list.
analysis.intuition: Deleting a node in a singly-linked list requires re-linking its predecessor node's `next` pointer to skip the target node. However, if the head of the list itself needs to be removed, it has no predecessor, creating special edge cases. Introducing a dummy head node (`pHead`) before the actual head standardizes the deletion logic: every node, including the original head, now has a non-null preceding node (`prev`), allowing us to cleanly bypass target nodes without extra conditional checks for the start of the list.
approach: Instantiate a dummy node `pHead` with value `0` and set `pHead.next = head`.
Initialize pointer `prev` to point to `pHead` and pointer `curr` to point to `head`.
Traverse the linked list using a `while` loop until `curr` becomes `null`.
If `curr.val == val`, remove `curr` by setting `prev.next = curr.next` without advancing `prev` (since the new `prev.next` might also contain `val`).
Advance `curr` to `curr.next` in every iteration to evaluate the next node.
Return `pHead.next`, which points to the updated head of the list.
analysis.why_it_works: The dummy head guarantees that `prev` always references a valid node whose value is confirmed not to equal `val`. When a target node is identified (`curr.val == val`), setting `prev.next = curr.next` effectively unlinks `curr` from the list structure. Keeping `prev` stationary during a deletion ensures that if consecutive nodes contain `val`, they are all continuously bypassed until a non-matching node is reached.
analysis.key_takeaway: Using a dummy (sentinel) head node simplifies linked list modifications by ensuring every node has a valid predecessor, eliminating special edge cases for head updates.
analysis.time_explanation: The solution visits each of the n nodes in the linked list exactly once in a single pass.
analysis.space_explanation: The algorithm operates in-place, using only a single dummy node and two pointer references regardless of input size.
